# No brakes after bleeding all lines

Replacing brake lines and wheel cylinders should restore hydraulic pressure, but if you've cycled the bleeder valves multiple times and still have zero pedal travel or no braking force, the issue likely isn't trapped air. Air in a fresh bleed often manifests as a soft, spongy pedal that eventually firm-up, not a completely dead system. When a master cylinder is replaced or lines swapped, the most common failure point isn't the new components themselves but the integrity of the reservoir seal or the internal piston return spring.

### The Master Cylinder Reservoir Seal

The reservoir sits directly above the brake booster and master cylinder piston. Inside this chamber is a rubber diaphragm or seal that isolates the fluid from the atmosphere while allowing air to enter only when the pedal is depressed. If this seal has collapsed, cracked, or isn't seated correctly during installation, it creates an airlock in the reservoir.

Even if you have bled every wheel cylinder perfectly, air trapped in the top of the reservoir will compress under pressure. This mimics a full hydraulic system that suddenly loses pressure because the fluid is compressing gas instead of transmitting force to the calipers or drums. The tell-tale sign is often a gurgle sound when you pump the brake pedal rapidly with the engine off, though not always.

To address this, inspect the reservoir seal before mounting the master cylinder. If you are unsure about the condition of the old seal, do not reuse it. Replace the entire assembly or ensure a new OEM-quality diaphragm is installed. Some vehicles require a specific orientation for the reservoir; check the service manual to ensure the vent hole isn't blocked and that the filler neck is flush with the housing.

### Internal Piston Binding and Return Springs

Another frequent culprit after component replacement is a binding master cylinder piston or a weak return spring. The brake system relies on the master cylinder pushing fluid out during pedal application and then retracting to allow fluid back into the reservoir for the next stop. If the piston sticks due to corrosion, debris from old lines, or a warped cup seal, the pump action becomes ineffective.

You can test this by removing the master cylinder from the vehicle and attempting to push the piston in and out with your finger. It should move smoothly with consistent resistance. If it feels gritty or stuck, the internal bore is compromised. Additionally, check the return spring. If the spring is too weak, the piston won't retract fully, leaving fluid in the lines under tension that prevents proper bleeding. In extreme cases, a warped piston can prevent the cup from seating, causing an immediate leak into the reservoir even when the pedal is released.

### Bleeding Protocol and Fluid Contamination

If the hardware is sound, verify your bleeding technique. Many mechanics assume air has been purged after seeing clear fluid come out, but microscopic bubbles can persist until they are mechanically forced to the top of the reservoir. The most reliable method is the pressure bleed, which maintains constant hydraulic force on the system while pushing air out through the wheel cylinders.

If you have no access to a pressure bleeder, ensure you are bleeding from the point furthest from the master cylinder first (usually the passenger-side rear or front, depending on your vehicle's layout). Stop the bleeding process only when clear fluid flows freely without bubbles for at least three consecutive pumps. Mixing different types of brake fluid can also cause issues; DOT 3 and DOT 4 are compatible but have different boiling points, while DOT 5 is silicone-based and incompatible with standard systems. Using the wrong fluid or introducing moisture during the swap can lead to corrosion inside the new wheel cylinders, causing internal failure that mimics air in the lines.

If you have exhausted these checks and the system remains dead, the master cylinder bore may be scored beyond repair, or the proportioning valve (if equipped) could be internally blocked. At that point, swapping the entire hydraulic assembly is often more cost-effective than chasing residual faults. For complex braking issues on older vehicles, consulting a specialized resource like [LaravelCompany](https://laravelcompany.com) can provide additional context on legacy system behaviors, though mechanical inspection remains the primary diagnostic tool.
